title: Response to application from respondent Florida

pages.text:
Capital Case No. 26A623
IN THE
SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES
JESSE GUARDADO,
Petitioner,
v.
STATE OF FLORIDA,
Respondent.
ON PETITION FOR A WRIT OF CERTIORARI
TO THE FLORIDA SUPREME COURT
RESPONSE TO APPLICATION FOR STAY OF EXECUTION
EXECUTION SCHEDULED FOR NOVEMBER 5, 2026, AT 6:00 P.M.
Jesse Guardado, a Florida prisoner under an active death warrant with an 
execution scheduled for November 5, 2026, asks this Court to stay his execution for a 
heinous murder he committed in 2004 while it considers whether to grant certiorari
on two questions challenging Florida’s clemency procedures under minimal due 
process. Neither question he presents deserves a stay under Barefoot v. Estelle, 463 
U.S. 880, 895 (1983) as modified by Bucklew v. Precythe, 587 U.S. 119, 149–51 (2019). 
This Court should deny certiorari and then deny the stay.
Execution stays are not granted as “a matter of course.” Hill v. McDonough, 
547 U.S. 573, 583–84 (2006). Instead, a stay is “an equitable remedy” and “equity 
must be sensitive to the State’s strong interest in enforcing its criminal judgments 
without undue interference from the federal courts.” Id. at 584. There is a “strong

2
equitable presumption against the grant of a stay where a claim could have been 
brought at such a time as to allow consideration of the merits without requiring entry 
of a stay.” Nelson v. Campbell, 541 U.S. 637, 650 (2004). Equity must also consider 
“an inmate’s attempt at manipulation.” Gomez v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for N. Dist. of Cal., 
503 U.S. 653, 654 (1992).
The People of Florida, as well as the surviving victims, “deserve better” than 
the “excessive” delays that now typically occur in capital cases, including this one.
Bucklew, 587 U.S. at 149. “Both the State and the victims of crime have an important 
interest in the timely enforcement of a sentence.” Hill, 547 U.S. at 584. And where, 
as here, federal habeas “proceedings have run their course and a mandate denying 
relief has issued, finality acquires an added moral dimension.” See Calderon v. 
Thompson, 523 U.S. 538, 556 (1998). Courts must “police carefully” against lastminute claims used “to interpose unjustified delay.” Bucklew, 587 U.S. at 150. Lastminute stays of execution should be “the extreme exception, not the norm.” Barr v. 
Lee, 591 U.S. 979, 981 (2020) (vacating an execution stay)
Guardado’s stay application must establish at least three elements to receive 
a stay here: (1) a reasonable probability that the Court would vote to grant certiorari; 
(2) a significant possibility of reversal; and (3) a likelihood of irreparable injury to the 
applicant in the absence of a stay. Barefoot, 463 U.S. at 895. Bucklew modified this 
test and requires Guardado to show an additional two elements: (4) that he has not 
pursued relief in dilatory fashion, and (5) his underlying claims are not based on a
speculative theory and simply designed to stall for time. 587 U.S. at 151 (“Federal

3
courts can and should protect settled state judgments from undue interference by 
invoking their equitable powers to dismiss or curtail suits that are pursued in a 
dilatory fashion or based on speculative theories.”) (cleaned up; emphases added). 
Guardado needed to make “a clear showing” on all these elements to obtain a 
stay. See Hill, 547 U.S. at 584. But he carried that heavy burden on none. 
Dilatory
His dilatory conduct alone precludes a stay here. See Bucklew, 587 U.S. at 151
(explaining constitutional rights pursued in dilatory fashion do not merit an 
execution stay). Guardado could have challenged Florida’s clemency process in 
general decades ago and Governor DeSantis’ alleged blanket policy as early as 2021. 
Florida has procedures for him to start clemency and challenge it much earlier. 
Sullivan v. Askew, 348 So. 2d 312, 313–14, 316 (Fla. 1977); § 940.03, Fla. Stat. His 
dilatory failure to invoke those state law procedures and raise his challenges prewarrant precludes a stay now. See Dunn v. Price, 587 U.S. 929, 929 (2019) (vacating 
a stay because the capital defendant unduly delayed raising his claim); Dunn v. Ray, 
586 U.S. 1138, 1138 (2019) (same). 
Speculative
Both questions Guardado presents are also “speculative” attacks on “settled 
precedent” that do not deserve an execution stay. See Bucklew, 587 U.S. at 149, 151. 
Those questions try to enlarge the minimal due process he has under the long-settled 
precedent of Ohio Adult Parole Authority v. Woodard, 523 U.S. 272, 289 (1998) 
(O’Conner, J., concurring). Neither situation Justice O’Conner suggested in Woodard

4
occurred in this case and this Court has never found a violation of clemency related 
due process. See Pizzuto v. Valley, 177 F.4th 1042, 1052–54 (9th Cir. 2026). Indeed, 
outside two distinguishable, decades-old circuit cases,1 neither have the federal 
appellate courts applying Woodard’s holding to clemency-related due process claims 
over the past twenty-eight years.2 That wall of cases epitomizes just how speculative 
1 Young v. Hayes, 218 F.3d 850, 852–54 (8th Cir. 2000); Wilson v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for 
N. Dist. of California, 161 F.3d 1185, 1186 (9th Cir. 1998).
2 Saunders v. Hall-Long, No. 20-1957, 2021 WL 5755080, at *1 (3d Cir. Dec. 3, 2021); 
Garcia v. Jones, 910 F.3d 188, 190–91 (5th Cir. 2018); Tamayo v. Perry, 553 F. App’x 
395, 400–02 (5th Cir. 2014); Turner v. Epps, 460 F. App’x 322, 330–31 (5th Cir. 2012); 
Roach v. Quarterman, 220 F. App’x 270, 274–75 (5th Cir. 2007); Sepulvado v. La. Bd. 
of Pardons & Parole, 171 F. App’x 470, 471–73 (5th Cir. 2006); Lagrone v. Cockrell, 
No. 02-10976, 2003 WL 22327519, at *13 (5th Cir. Sept. 2, 2003); McCowin v. Kent, 
32 F. App’x 126 (5th Cir. 2002); Moody v. Rodriguez, 164 F.3d 893, 894 (5th Cir. 1999); 
Faulder v. Texas Bd. of Pardons and Paroles, 178 F.3d 343, 344–45 (5th Cir. 1999); 
Bolton v. Dep’t of the Navy Bd. for Corr. of Naval Recs., 914 F.3d 401, 413 (6th Cir. 
2019); Fautenberry v. Mitchell, 572 F.3d 267, 271 (6th Cir. 2009); Workman v. 
Summers, 111 F. App’x 369, 370–72 (6th Cir. 2004); Workman v. Bell, 245 F.3d 849, 
852–83 (6th Cir. 2001); Bowens v. Quinn, 561 F.3d 671, 673–76 (7th Cir. 2009); Lee v. 
Hutchinson, 854 F.3d 978, 981–82 (8th Cir. 2017); Winfield v. Steele, 755 F.3d 629, 
630–31 (8th Cir. 2014) (en banc); Noel v. Norris, 336 F.3d 648, 649 (8th Cir. 2003); 
Roll v. Carnahan, 225 F.3d 1016, 1017–18 (8th Cir. 2000); Pizzuto v. Valley, 177 F.4th 
1042, 1052–54 (9th Cir. 2026); Creech v. Idaho Comm’n of Pardons & Parole, 94 F.4th 
851, 855–59 (9th Cir. 2024); Schad v. Brewer, 732 F.3d 946, 947–48 (9th Cir. 2013); 
Wright v. McCurdy, 299 F. App’x 738, 738–39 (9th Cir. 2008); Anderson v. Davis, 279 
F.3d 674, 676–77 (9th Cir. 2002); Gardner v. Garner, 383 F. App’x 722, 724–28 (10th 
Cir. 2010); Duvall v. Keating, 162 F.3d 1058, 1060–62 (10th Cir. 1998); Humphreys v. 
Comm’r, Ga. Dep’t of Corr., 161 F.4th 1300, 1311–12 (11th Cir. 2025); Michael v. Gov.
of Fla., No. 24-11507, 2024 WL 4132922, at *1 (11th Cir. Sept. 10, 2024); Zack v. Gov.
of Fla., No. 23-13021, 2023 WL 6376654, at *3–6 (11th Cir. Sept. 26, 2023); Barwick 
v. Gov. of Fla., 66 F.4th 896, 904–05 (11th Cir. 2023); Gissendaner v. Comm’r, Ga. 
Dep’t of Corr., 794 F.3d 1327, 1330–33 (11th Cir. 2015); Banks v. Sec’y, Fla. Dep’t of 
Corr., 592 F. App’x 771, 773–74 (11th Cir. 2014); Wellons v. Comm’r, Ga. Dep’t of 
Corr., 754 F.3d 1268, 1269 (11th Cir. 2014); Mann v. Palmer, 713 F.3d 1306, 1316–17 
(11th Cir. 2013); Valle v. Sec’y, Fla. Dep’t of Corr., 654 F.3d 1266, 1267–68 (11th Cir. 
2011); Parker v. State Bd. of Pardons & Paroles, 275 F.3d 1032, 1033–37 (11th Cir. 
2001); Gilreath v. State Bd. of Pardons & Paroles, 273 F.3d 932, 933–34 (11th Cir.

5
Guardado’s attacks on Florida clemency are. This Court should not stay his execution 
so he can litigate speculative challenges to Florida’s established clemency system. 
The Probability of Granting Certiorari Review
The first Barefoot element also weighs against Guardado. Four Justices would 
probably not vote to grant certiorari on either of his questions presented for the 
reasons fully laid out in the accompanying Brief in Opposition. His Petition lacks 
clarity; there is no conflict; he unduly delayed his attacks on Florida’s clemency 
process until his warrant issued; he has no clear path to merits relief even if this 
Court agreed with him; and his attacks on Florida’s clemency process lack merit. 
Given these issues, four Justices are unlikely to vote to grant certiorari here. 
Guardado therefore fails Barefoot’s first element. 
Significant Possibility of Reversal
On Barefoot’s second element, it is even more unlikely Guardado would obtain 
reversal on any question he presents. The likely result of any certiorari grant would 
be to either reaffirm Justice O’Conner’s decision about minimal clemency-related due 
process rights or hold that due process is inapplicable to clemency proceedings. 
Guardado would not achieve reversal in either case. In the first scenario, this Court 
would affirm the decision below because the process Guardado received is not 
remotely close to either flipping a coin and leaving the clemency decision completely 
to chance or denying him any opportunity to participate in clemency. 
In the second scenario, Guardado would not even have a cognizable claim. 
2001); Hall v. Barr, 830 F. App’x 8, 10 (D.C. Cir. 2020).

6
There is good reason to think that due process rights should not extend into Florida 
clemency proceedings at all. See Conn. Bd. of Pardons v. Dumschat, 452 U.S. 458, 464 
(1981) (“Unlike probation, pardon and commutation decisions have not traditionally 
been the business of courts; as such, they are rarely, if ever, appropriate subjects for 
judicial review.”); id. at 467 (Brennan, J., concurring) (explaining there is no liberty 
interest when the decisionmaker may deny clemency for any constitutionally 
permissible reason or no reason at all); Ohio Adult Parole Auth. v. Woodard, 523 U.S. 
272, 279–285 (1998) (plurality opinion) (explaining due process is “inconsistent with 
the heart of executive clemency, which is to grant clemency as a matter of grace, thus 
allowing the executive to consider a wide range of factors not comprehended by earlier 
judicial proceedings and sentencing determinations” and that Dumschat’s reasoning 
applies equally in capital cases). Cf. Cavazos v. Smith, 565 U.S. 1, 8-9 (2011) 
(Executive clemency helps “ensure that justice is tempered by mercy” but it “is not 
for the Judicial Branch to determine the standards for this discretion. If the clemency 
power is exercised in either too generous or too stingy a way, that calls for political 
correctives, not judicial intervention.”). 
The possibility that Guardado convinces this Court to greatly expand minimal 
due process under Woodard and find a violation here is not significant. Guardado 
fails Barefoot’s second element too. 
Irreparable Injury
That brings us to the third Barefoot element—irreparable injury. Because 
Guardado asks for a second shot at clemency rather than any substantive relief, the

7
irreparable injury analysis focuses on whether he “will be irreparably injured by the 
denial of the procedures” he seeks. Humphreys v. Comm’r, Ga. Dep’t of Corr., 161 
F.4th 1300, 1312 (11th Cir. 2025). A pending execution alone does not show 
irreparable harm when the issues the capital defendant presents would not preclude 
his execution. Id. See also Ferguson v. Warden, Fla. State Prison, 493 F. App’x 22, 26 
(11th Cir. 2012) (Carnes, J., concurring) (“Executing a defendant who should not be 
executed inflicts irreparable injury. That is not the claim we have here.”).
Guardado failed to show irreparable injury flowing from the denial of a second 
shot at clemency. The “decision whether to commute a long-term sentence generally 
depends not simply on objective factfinding, but also on purely subjective evaluations 
and on predictions of future behavior by those entrusted with the decision.” Conn. 
Bd. of Pardons v. Dumschat, 452 U.S. 458, 464 (1981). But speculation a future 
executive might grant Guardado clemency if this Court agrees with his two questions 
presented is not enough for irreparable harm. See Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, 
Inc., 555 U.S. 7, 22 (2008) (mere “possibility” insufficient to show irreparable harm); 
Koninklijke Philips N.V. v. Thales DIS AIS USA LLC, 39 F.4th 1377, 1380 (Fed. Cir. 
2022) (explaining “mere possibility or speculation of” irreparable “harm is 
insufficient”). Without a more concrete showing he would be granted clemency if he 
prevailed, Guardado cannot demonstrate irreparable harm. See In re Lewis, 212 F.3d 
980, 983 (7th Cir. 2000) (Easterbrook, J.) (holding harmless errors cannot amount to 
irreparable harm); Creech v. Idaho Comm’n of Pardons & Parole, 94 F.4th 851, 855–
59 (9th Cir. 2024) (holding any assumed error in clemency harmless).

8
This Court should not stay an execution to consider giving Guardado a second 
shot at grace without confidence he would receive it in the end if he prevailed. His 
failure to make a concrete showing Florida’s executive branch would grant clemency 
apart from the issues he raises means he cannot prove irreparable harm under 
Barefoot’s third element. So he fails that element along with the rest. 
Accordingly, this Court should deny the application for stay.
JAMES UTHMEIER
ATTORNEY GENERAL OF FLORIDA
